place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育馆 · 十月三十一日

setup.zh: 队内对抗赛，板凳上坐了五十七分钟，末尾两罚；雷老师喊「深吸一口！憋住！」，一个没进。傍晚空球馆，阿禾把他的指头按在他自己腕子上：吸四拍，吐六拍——吐是踩刹车。
setup.en: The scrimmage: fifty-seven minutes on the bench, then two free throws at the end; Coach Lei shouts "Big breath! Hold it!", and neither goes in. In the empty gym at dusk Ahe sets his fingers on his own wrist: in for four, out for six — breathing out is the brake.

recap.zh: 罚球 0/2，出手前憋气；砍鲨；阿禾教他吸四吐六——吐是踩刹车，刹得住一截。
recap.en: Free throws 0/2, breath held before the shot; hack-a-Shaq; Ahe taught him in-four, out-six — breathing out is the brake, and it holds back a notch.

zh: 两罚，手环上一个数：一百四十一。
en: Two shots; one number on the band: 141.
In for four, out for six.

story.zh:
十月三十日夜里，院系杯的名单进了群：针推院队报了十二个人，他是第十二个；中锋是大刘——九月跑去街舞社、叫阿禾一张报名表拉回来的那个一米八八。马小宝回中药学院，站到了对面。底下还转来学院一张通知，老蔡念给他听：「各院队以院系杯名次核定下一年度经费；未进前四者，不再单独组队。」针推去年第六。表上「领队」那一栏，签的是阿禾的名字——这支队，是她一个学院一个学院跑下来、一张一张报名表拉起来的。

第二天早上，他揣着一个球想去球馆先投几个。球馆门锁着，门上一张纸：「下午对抗赛，上午保洁。」他只好在宿舍楼下的水泥地上，对着一棵梧桐树比划出手的姿势，比划到第二十几下，六楼一扇窗开了，老蔡探出半个身子，拿手机对着他：「来，忙哥，再来一个，我开着直播呢。」「你直播什么？」「宿舍群。眼镜说要科学分析你的出手角度。」窗户里眼镜的声音传出来：「我没说。我说的是，他抬肘的时候，手腕是歪的。」沈芒把球往怀里一抱，不比划了。手腕歪不歪，他没敢低头看。

十月三十一日下午，队内对抗赛。馆门口新贴了一张通知：「十二月一日至十五日，球馆换地板。」没人多看一眼。

看台上坐了小一百号人。队内对抗赛向来没人看，这一回不知怎么传开了，说院系杯名单刚交，各学院的人都来瞧瞧校队里谁是谁。中药学院来了一排，人人一件新球衣，胸口「马氏大药房」四个字在灯底下晃得人眼晕。老蔡和眼镜坐在第三排，老蔡手里一袋瓜子，眼镜手里一本书。

沈芒坐在白队板凳的最末，坐了五十七分钟。这五十七分钟里，他捡了十九个球，递了三十一瓶水，鼓了不知多少回掌，掌心都拍红了。他还看了马小宝罚六个球。

马小宝罚球跟喝水一样。他走上线，先冲看台挥一挥手，看台上便有人尖叫；拍一下球，扭头跟裁判说句笑话，裁判也忍不住笑；然后随手一抛，「唰」，连筐都不碰。六个进了五个。投丢的那一个，他自己先笑出了声，冲看台一摊手，看台上笑得比他投进的时候还响。

沈芒坐在板凳上看得心里发凉。他看明白了一件事：那一圈眼睛，到了马小宝身上是暖气；到了他身上，是冰窖。

然后，事情一件接一件，像有人排好了的：队长邢斌第五次犯规下场；白队的大前锋一个急停，小腿抽了筋，抱着腿在地上打滚；一个上半场戳伤了手指，缠得像一根胡萝卜；一个刚去上厕所没回来；另两个替补有实验课，没来。红队五十八，白队五十七，表上只剩零点几秒。雷老师看了看表，又看了看板凳，板凳上只剩一个人。

他朝那个人一摆手：「0号！上！」

沈芒站起来，腿是软的。雷老师一把扯住他的球衣，压低了嗓子吼：「接了球，传！随便传给谁！别运，别投，别想！」他点头如捣蒜。走上场，看台上「哦——」了一声，拖得很长，有人笑，有人举起了手机。

白队后场发球，球传到他手里。他接住了——这已经是他今天最大的成就——还没想好往哪儿跑，一面墙便压了过来。马小宝伸手往他怀里一掏，像在抢球，掏完了两条胳膊顺势一合，结结实实抱了他一下，亲热得像在火车站接一个远房亲戚。哨响。红队这一节的犯规早满了，犯一个，便是两罚。马小宝冲裁判举手：「我的，我的。」又低头冲他笑：「送你上罚球线。」

两罚。

那条白线，他在场边看了一个月，从没觉得它有多远；这时候站上去，只觉得篮筐在一百里外，又小又高，像挂在天上的一只碗。看台上小一百号人，没了声。没了，比有还吓人。他听得见自己的心，咚，咚，快得像楼上有人跺地板。手环上一个数：一百四十一。

他拍了两下球。球是湿的——是他的手心湿了。

头一个，球从筐前直直掉下去，连筐都没碰。看台炸了，有人笑出了眼泪，有人喊「三不沾」，第三排老蔡把瓜子撒了一地。

板凳那头两个声音一齐到。雷老师的嗓门大：「深吸一口！憋住！」阿禾的不高，不急：「吐气！」

他听了嗓门大的那个，深深吸了一口，憋住，脖子都粗了，把第二个投了出去。「当」，砸在筐前沿上。终场哨响。

马小宝走过来在他后背上拍了两拍，拍得他往前一冲，声音不大，看台前三排都听得见：「院系杯上，我还犯你。犯你一回，送你两个。」看台上又笑开了。沈芒没听出这句话有什么好笑。他听出来的是一个打法：往后哪一场比赛，只要他在场上，对面便不防他、不抢他，只抱他；抱一回，他便站上这条线，一个人，四面八方全是眼睛。

输的一队周日早上扫球馆；白队的人散场时把扫帚往他怀里一塞：「你罚的，你扫。」周日早上七点球馆门口全是晨练的人，他不想当着他们扫。于是这天傍晚，空荡荡的球馆里，只剩一个人、一把扫帚，和一张折叠桌后头的一个领队。

阿禾在对账。院系杯八个学院的队服、场地、裁判，全在她那个本子上，计算器按得嗒嗒响。翻到某一页她停了停，添了一行，沈芒扫到桌边伸长了脖子瞥见：「沈芒　罚球 0/2　出手前憋气。」

「那叫砍鲨。」阿禾头也不抬，「当年美国那个最大块头的中锋奥尼尔，力气大得能把篮架拽下来，就是罚球不行，对面专门派人去犯他：抱他，拉他，让他上线，投丢一个，白赚一个球权。」

「那我跟奥尼尔，一个待遇。」

「人家两米一六。」她放下笔，「过来。伸手。」

沈芒把扫帚靠在桌边。她把他右手翻过来，手心朝上，又把他左手两根指头拉过来，按在他右手腕子大拇指那一侧：「别看手环，摸。」

他摸着了。一跳，一跳。

「慢慢吸，四拍。」

他吸。吸到第三拍，指头底下那一跳一跳，紧了，快了一点。

「慢慢吐，六拍。」

吐到一半，那跳松了，一下和一下隔得长了，像走路的人放慢了步子。心跳果然缓和了下来。他又吸，又快了；又吐，又慢了。他瞪着眼看她，像个头一回发现自己有影子的小孩：「它……跟着我喘气走？」

「本来就是这样。吸气的时候心跳快一点，吐气的时候慢一点，人人都是。」阿禾道，「吸是踩油门，吐是踩刹车。吐得比吸的长，心就慢一截。」

解剖台上那两根白线，忽然在他指头底下动了一下。老师说的，吐气的时候它说得多一点——原来是这个。

「你上线，一百四十一，然后吸一大口，憋住。」阿禾拿笔点了点本子，「憋着，刹车是踩不下去的。吐出来那一下，才是刹车。」

「那吐一口，就不抖了？」

「不是。」她答得很快，「人一怕，身子里放出来的那股东西，几分钟才退得下去，吐一口气退不完。可是能压下去一截。一截，就够你把球投到篮筐上。出手前，先长长地吐一口气，吐得比吸的长。吐完了，再投。」

「吐气我会。补测那天，我就是吐着跑完的。」

「我知道。那天你会，今天一站上线，就忘了。」她顿了顿，「再说，那天你吐，是把肺里的旧气倒干净，好让新气进来——那是跑步的吐。今天的吐，是踩刹车的吐。一口气，两样用处。」

沈芒想起压在抽屉里、从古籍部抄回来的那一页：「我抄的那本古书上，吸一种，吐六种。」

「六种，」阿禾道，「都是吐。」

她看了他一眼。这一眼跟平日里看一个数的眼神，有一点不一样。她低下头，又添了一笔。
story.en:
On the night of October the thirtieth the roster for the College Cup came into the group chat: the Acupuncture and Tuina college team entered twelve players, and he was the twelfth; the centre was Big Liu — the six-foot-two who'd run off to the street-dance club in September and been hauled back by Ahe with one sign-up form. Ma Xiaobao went back to the Chinese Pharmacy college and lined up on the other side. Under it someone had forwarded a notice from the college, and Old Cai read it out to him: "Each college team's funding for next year will be set by its College Cup placing; any college outside the top four will no longer field its own team." Acupuncture had come sixth last year. In the "Team manager" box the signature was Ahe's — this team was one she had pulled together college by college, sign-up form by sign-up form.

The next morning he tucked a ball under his arm to go and get a few shots up in the gym first. The gym door was locked, a sheet of paper on it: "Scrimmage this afternoon; cleaning this morning." So he stood on the concrete outside the dorm and practised his shooting form at a plane tree; around the twenty-somethingth rep a window opened on the sixth floor and Old Cai leaned half out of it, phone pointed at him: "Come on, Busy, one more, I'm streaming." "Streaming what?" "The room group. Specs said he wanted to scientifically analyse your release angle." Specs's voice came through the window: "I didn't. I said when he lifts his elbow, his wrist is crooked." Shen Mang hugged the ball to his chest and stopped. Whether his wrist was crooked, he didn't dare look down to see.

The afternoon of October the thirty-first, an intra-squad scrimmage. A new notice was taped to the gym door: "December 1st to 15th, gym floor replacement." Nobody gave it a second look.

A hundred-odd people sat in the stands. Nobody ever came to watch an intra-squad scrimmage, but this time word had got round somehow that the College Cup rosters were just in and every college had come to see who was who on the school team. Chinese Pharmacy had sent a whole row, every one in a new jersey with "Ma's Pharmacy" across the chest, dazzling under the lights. Old Cai and Specs sat in the third row, Old Cai with a bag of sunflower seeds, Specs with a book.

Shen Mang sat at the end of the White bench for fifty-seven minutes. In those fifty-seven minutes he fetched nineteen balls, handed out thirty-one bottles of water and clapped more times than he could count, until his palms were red. He also watched Ma Xiaobao shoot six free throws.

Ma Xiaobao shot free throws the way other people drank water. He walked to the line and waved at the stands first, and someone in the stands screamed; he bounced the ball once, turned to tell the referee a joke, and the referee couldn't help laughing; then he flipped it up without looking — swish, never touched the rim. Five of six. The one he missed, he laughed at first himself, spread his hands at the stands, and the stands laughed louder than when he'd made them.

Shen Mang sat on the bench and went cold inside. He had understood one thing: that ring of eyes was a radiator for Ma Xiaobao; for him, it was an icebox.

Then things happened one after another, as if someone had lined them up: the captain, Xing Bin, picked up his fifth foul and sat; White's power forward pulled up short, his calf cramped, and he rolled on the floor clutching it; one had jammed a finger in the first half, taped up like a carrot; one had just gone to the toilet and not come back; the other two reserves had a lab class and hadn't come. Red fifty-eight, White fifty-seven, a few tenths of a second left on the clock. Coach Lei looked at the clock, then at the bench, and there was one person left on it.

He waved at that person: "Number zero! In!"

Shen Mang stood up, and his legs were soft. Coach Lei grabbed a fistful of his jersey and roared in an undertone: "Catch it, pass! Pass to anyone! Don't dribble, don't shoot, don't think!" He nodded like a pestle. As he walked onto the court the stands went "Ohhh —", long drawn out; some laughed, some raised their phones.

White inbounded from the backcourt, and the ball came to him. He caught it — already his greatest achievement of the day — and before he'd decided where to run, a wall bore down on him. Ma Xiaobao reached into his arms as if going for the ball, and having reached, closed both arms and gave him a solid hug, as warmly as meeting a distant cousin at the railway station. Whistle. Red had long since used up its fouls for the quarter; one more meant two free throws. Ma Xiaobao raised his hand to the ref: "Mine, mine." Then he grinned down at him: "Off you go to the line."

Two shots.

That white line — he'd watched it from the sideline for a month and never thought it far; standing on it now, the basket was a hundred miles away, small and high, like a bowl hung in the sky. The hundred-odd people in the stands went quiet. Quiet was worse than noise. He could hear his own heart, thump, thump, fast as someone stamping on the floor upstairs. A number on his fitness band: a hundred and forty-one.

He bounced the ball twice. The ball was wet — his palms were wet.

The first one dropped straight down in front of the rim without touching it. The stands erupted; someone laughed till they cried, someone yelled "Air ball!", and in the third row Old Cai spilled his sunflower seeds all over the floor.

From the bench two voices arrived at once. Coach Lei's was loud: "Deep breath! Hold it!" Ahe's was not loud, not hurried: "Breathe out!"

He listened to the loud one, took a deep breath, held it till his neck swelled, and put up the second. Clang, off the front of the rim. The final whistle blew.

Ma Xiaobao came over and slapped him twice on the back, hard enough to pitch him forward, not loud, but the first three rows could hear: "College Cup, I'll foul you again. Every foul, two free ones for you." The stands laughed again. Shen Mang couldn't hear what was funny about it. What he heard was a game plan: in any match from now on, as long as he was on the court, the other side wouldn't guard him or go for the ball — they'd just hug him; one hug, and he'd be standing on this line, alone, eyes on every side.

The losing team swept the gym on Sunday morning; as the White players left, they shoved the broom into his arms: "Your free throws. You sweep." At seven on a Sunday morning the gym door was full of people doing their morning exercise, and he didn't want to sweep in front of them. So at dusk that day the empty gym held one person, one broom, and one team manager behind a folding table.

Ahe was doing the accounts. Jerseys, courts and referees for all eight colleges in the College Cup were in that notebook, and her calculator clicked away. On one page she paused and added a line; Shen Mang swept his way to the table and craned his neck: "Shen Mang   FT 0/2   Held breath before release."

"That's called hack-a-Shaq," Ahe said without looking up. "Back in the day the biggest centre in America, O'Neal, strong enough to pull a hoop down, couldn't shoot free throws, so the other side sent people to foul him on purpose: hug him, grab him, put him on the line; every miss was a free possession."

"So I get the same treatment as O'Neal."

"He's seven foot one." She put down her pen. "Come here. Hold out your hand."

Shen Mang leaned the broom against the table. She turned his right hand palm up, then took two fingers of his left hand and set them on his right wrist, on the thumb side: "Don't look at the band. Feel it."

He found it. A beat. A beat.

"Breathe in slowly. Four counts."

He breathed in. At the third count, the beat under his fingers tightened and quickened a little.

"Breathe out slowly. Six counts."

Halfway through the breath out, the beat loosened, longer between one and the next, like a walker slowing his pace. His heartbeat really had slowed down. In again, and it quickened; out again, and it slowed. He stared at her like a child who has just found out he has a shadow: "It... follows my breathing?"

"That's how it is. The heart's a little faster when you breathe in, a little slower when you breathe out; everyone's is," said Ahe. "Breathing in is the accelerator, breathing out is the brake. Breathe out longer than you breathe in and your heart slows a notch."

The two white threads on the dissection table moved, suddenly, under his fingers. What the instructor had said — when you breathe out, it speaks a little more — so this was it.

"You stepped up to the line at a hundred and forty-one, then took a huge breath and held it." Ahe tapped her notebook with the pen. "While you're holding it, you can't press the brake. The moment you let it out — that's the brake."

"So one breath out, and I stop shaking?"

"No." She answered fast. "When you're afraid, the stuff your body releases takes minutes to fade; one breath out doesn't clear it. But it can press it down a notch. One notch is enough to get the ball to the rim. Before you shoot, one long breath out, longer than the breath in. Then shoot."

"I can breathe out. On the retest I ran the whole way breathing out."

"I know. You could that day; today you stepped on the line and forgot." She paused. "Besides, that day you breathed out to empty the old air from your lungs so new air could come in — that's a runner's breath. Today's breath out is a brake. One breath, two uses."

Shen Mang thought of the page he'd copied in the rare-books room, pressed in his drawer: "The old book I copied — one way in, six ways out."

"Six ways," said Ahe, "all of them out."

She looked at him. That look was a little different from the way she looked at a number. She bent her head and added another line.

exits.means: breathes in for four and out for six and shoots

refuse.zh: 心还在楼上跺地板。吸四拍，吐六拍。
refuse.en: His heart is still stamping upstairs. In for four, out for six.

story.zh:
他扫完了地，从球车里摸出一个球，走到那条白线上。馆里灯关了一半，篮筐在半明半暗里倒显得近了。他想起眼镜那句，抬肘时把手腕摆正。吸四拍，吐六拍；再吸，再吐。吐到第二口的末尾，心口那阵擂鼓似的跳慢了，手也稳了。出手。

进了。又进了。砸筐。又进了。

他心里一热，回头要喊，看见门口靠着一个人，一米九三，拎着落下的大摇杯，笑眯眯地看着。

他转回头，吸四，吐六，心口那一阵跳，怎么也慢不下来了。球砸在篮板上，弹得老远。

马小宝拧开摇杯喝了一口：「你看。有人看着，就不行。」晃着摇杯走了。

球滚到折叠桌底下。阿禾弯腰把球捡起来：「他说得对。没人看着，四个进三个；有人看着，一个进不了。光练投篮没用。从下礼拜起，每天练完，全队站在底线上，看着你投十个。投丢一个，全队陪你折返跑一趟。」

沈芒的脸一下子白了：「全队？看着？」

「全队。看着。」她把球塞回他怀里，「院系杯头一轮，十一月七号。看台上，比今天多十倍。」

他憋了半天，憋出一句：「他怎么就不怕？」

「怕的东西，各人不一样。他也有。」

「他怕什么？」

「不知道。没记过。」

这是他头一回听她说，有一样东西她没记过。

她拎起折叠桌走到门口，又回过头来：「今天喊你吐气那一下，你吸了。」

沈芒抱着球站在空球馆正当中，对着那条白线，又吐了一口长气。
story.en:
When he'd finished sweeping he fished a ball out of the cart and walked to that white line. Half the lights in the hall were off, and in the half-dark the basket looked closer. He remembered what Specs had said, and set his wrist straight as he raised his elbow. In for four, out for six; in again, out again. Towards the end of the second breath out, the drumming in his chest slowed, and his hands steadied. He shot.

In. In again. Off the rim. In again.

Something hot rose in him; he turned to shout, and saw someone leaning in the doorway, six foot four, carrying the big shaker he'd left behind, watching with a smile.

He turned back, in for four, out for six, and the pounding in his chest would not slow down no matter what. The ball smashed off the backboard and bounced far away.

Ma Xiaobao unscrewed his shaker and took a drink: "See. Someone's watching, and you can't." He swung the shaker and left.

The ball rolled under the folding table. Ahe bent down and picked it up: "He's right. Nobody watching, three of four; somebody watching, not one. So practising shooting on its own is no use. Starting next week, after every practice the whole team stands on the baseline and watches you shoot ten. Every miss, the whole team runs a suicide with you."

Shen Mang's face went white: "The whole team? Watching?"

"The whole team. Watching." She pushed the ball back into his arms. "First round of the College Cup, November the seventh. The stands will hold ten times today's."

He held it in a long while, and got out: "How come he's not afraid?"

"Everyone's afraid of different things. He has his too."

"What's he afraid of?"

"Don't know. Never recorded it."

It was the first time he had heard her say there was something she hadn't recorded.

She picked up the folding table and walked to the door, and turned back: "When I shouted 'breathe out' today — you breathed in."

Shen Mang stood in the middle of the empty gym with the ball in his arms, facing that white line, and let out one more long breath.
